I got annoyed last week that LLMs were writing haveI or letI in the middle of tactic proofs (this is not necessary, they should be have/let), and when I asked someone about this they asked me how often this occurred in mathlib (because that's what these things are trained on). Rather than just grepping for the answer I got Fable to write a linter #41562 to search for this. There are around 2300 occurrences of this in mathlib, but once a linter was flagging them it was easy to fix them all so I got Opus to do that and the result is #41615.

Side-topic, now resolved by #41664 :

I benched the code, expecting no changes, but the file Mathlib.FieldTheory.PurelyInseparable.PerfectClosure was consistently 13% slower. Intrigued, I got Claude to dig further, and I discovered that it seems to be the case that all but one of these 2300 changes have no effect whatsoever on timings, but this haveI on line 244 of the file https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/30ff0d59c48647f4d2f88c55fe92696464019c50/Mathlib/FieldTheory/PurelyInseparable/PerfectClosure.lean#L244 , if changed to a have, randomly makes kernel typechecking of docs#IntermediateField.adjoin_eq_adjoin_pow_expChar_pow_of_isSeparable double in time:

have:
[Elab.async] [20863870.000000] ✅️ _private.Lean.AddDecl.0.Lean.addDeclCore ▶

haveI:
[Elab.async] [11997950.000000] ✅️ _private.Lean.AddDecl.0.Lean.addDeclCore ▶

Because this is kernel typechecking, traces give me no further information. But I thought it was pretty surprising, given that (a) haveI and have are pretty much the same thing and (b) all the other 2300 changes seemed to have no effect at all.

This is not the first time that I have seen a completely innocuous-looking change in a proof which has made the kernel go crazy (the most famous example is universe renaming, which might now have been fixed). However every time it's somewhere deep in the algebra heirarchy and I find these things extremely difficult to minimise (and hence get the core team to take them seriously) and I cannot debug further myself because it's beyond my competence.

I suppose I could try mathlib-minimiser, perhaps this example isn't as deep in commutative algebra as some of the other examples I've seen...

Thanks, I think this is a good PR. I wonder if there is a way to make review easy (2300 is a somewhat large for a manual review), since this is an automatic change. Could we maybe generate this PR using skimmer, to be sure that it did the right thing? (cc @Thomas Murrills)

Just to be clear -- I would happily close or hand over this PR. I don't know what to think about the linter, especially as it is LLM-generated, but my main motivation for it was to check this PR hadn't missed anything. But the more we can automate this idea the better (eg Opus might have changed some things which didn't need changing)

If the linter produces try-this suggestions (which sounds faaairly easy for this problem?), then scripts/runSkimmer.sh will deterministically apply them :)

It will probably be easiest to review the linter to make sure the try-this suggestions are correct.

But, be careful, there's a bug where I mismanage the lake traces (which I plan to fix in the next couple weeks as I refocus back on skimmer). If you interrupt it halfway, be sure to remove .lake/build/skimmer/. (Once the bug is fixed that won't be necessary.)

As for the implementation of the linter in #41562, it does a search through the info tree, which will result in a performance overhead. A more efficient approach would be to overwrite the letI/haveI elaborators. This can be done for both the tactic and the term (your PR only does the tactic).

Of course even easier would be to make a PR to core so that we wouldn't need to overwrite any elaborators. I wonder if core would be happy to have such a linter.

You could also search the source syntax in a linter and only then look up info in the infotrees at the given source position(s), which is probably somewhere between the two in terms of performance, and is less invasive.

(It might also be slightly more robust? I can imagine that maybe the term-mode letI/haveI wouldn't have the fully de-metavariable'd type available during elaboration in certain circumstances, but the infotrees would?)

Another thing that I'm not sure the current PR handles correctly is multiple TacticInfos referring to the same source (as you'd have after <;>), where you should check that all of the goals are Props (and only have one try-this suggestion). Though this being a problem is a pretty unlikely edge case!
It is true that there may be metavariables, but I'd be really surprised if it wouldn't be able to tell that the universe is Prop during elaboration of the haveI/letI.
It's for sure an edge case, but what about universe metavariables?
Can you come up with a realistic example where it is not clear that the goal is a Prop after elaborating the value of the haveI/letI, but this becomes clear later?
Not without some thought, but I maintain a general concern about universes in category theory. :laughing:
If the elaboration of letI/haveI somehow precludes this, though, that would be neat.
I just noticed that the haveI/letI tactics are macros, so it's not so direct to add a Try this replacement suggestion from core either.

/-- `haveI` behaves like `have`, but inlines the value instead of producing a `have` term. -/
macro "haveI" c:letConfig d:letDecl : tactic => `(tactic| refine_lift haveI $c:letConfig $d:letDecl; ?_)

/-- `letI` behaves like `let`, but inlines the value instead of producing a `let` term. -/
macro "letI" c:letConfig d:letDecl : tactic => `(tactic| refine_lift letI $c:letConfig $d:letDecl; ?_)

@Kevin Buzzard I'm curious as to what happens if you try prompting Fable with something like this:

Please rewrite the linter to first find (the tactic and term version of) haveI/letI syntax in the source syntax examined by the linter, then look up the corresponding TacticInfo(s) or (Partial)TermInfo(s) for the relevant syntax range (which, note, may depend on whether we're looking at the term version or tactic version). If the goal is a proposition (following the current behavior), then add an interactive try-this suggestion that replaces the source syntax we found with have/let respectively. But instead of suggesting a replacement for the entire syntax range, target just the haveI/letI token's range and suggest the appropriate replacement string for the token (not syntax). This allows us to sidestep issues with pretty-printing and (re)formatting. Also, if there are multiple TacticInfos (or TermInfo(s)) for the position (as might be the case after <;>), ensure that all of them are Props. In general, we want to make sure that we attach only one try this suggestion per original source location, and that we give ourselves every chance to identify a propositional goal/term.

I haven't specified some things, but I wonder if Fable can figure out how to do them :)

I just noticed that we already have a have/let linter that warns about uses of have where the type is not a proposition, suggesting to use let instead.

Whatever we end up doing, it would be good to merge these into a single linter.
I have created #41657, which implements the linter in the way that I suggested above.

I pushed its response to your question @Thomas Murrills to #41562 ; Fable's explanation of the work can be seen here https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/41562/changes/f44a8e0534c6ac686cd0ebe02c80f81c0a40b129

Historical note: a lot of the haveI/letI usage is a remnant of Lean 3 times, where the I stood for Instances: the old versions of the have/let tactics would not add the new variable to the list of available instances, and you'd need haveI/letI to force an update to the instance cache and make them visible. In our modern Lean 4 age, basic have/let already make the instance available and I instead only stands for Inline. But the old haveI got ported to the new haveI and so there is a bit of a superstition that we have to keep upsing haveI and letI for instances.

Hmm, I'm totally unfamiliar with WSL, but Fable is telling me there might be some sort of memory issue that causes thrashing and causes hanging? Basically, too much lean file elaboration at once:

WSL turns "heavy" into "hung." Default WSL2 caps memory; overflow goes to a vhdx swap file, which thrashes instead of OOM-killing. And if the project lives on /mnt/c (DrvFs/9P), olean mmaps aren't shared page cache the way they are on ext4 — every exe pays full I/O and full private memory, 20–100× slower. This is exactly the "works-but-slow on Linux, freezes on WSL" signature.

And honestly, given how the scheduling works in skimmer and how much elaboration could get going, I wouldn't be surprised if that were the issue somehow. I'll need to think about that...

Here's the git diff responsible; the first new have is what fails. Original code:

/-- An object is initial if and only if its fiber is empty. -/
lemma initial_iff_fiber_empty (X : C) : Nonempty (IsInitial X) ↔ IsEmpty (F.obj X) := by
  rw [(IsInitial.isInitialIffObj F X).nonempty_congr]
  haveI : PreservesFiniteColimits (forget FintypeCat) := by
    change PreservesFiniteColimits FintypeCat.incl
    infer_instance
  haveI : ReflectsColimit (Functor.empty.{0} _) (forget FintypeCat) := by
    change ReflectsColimit (Functor.empty.{0} _) FintypeCat.incl
    infer_instance

(The linter suggests replacing both haveIs.)
Interestingly, deleting both of these haveIs outright is fine now.

Related to this, I have also created #41759 which deprecates the haveI' and letI' do-elements. I don't think there is any good enough reason to use these over just have or let. Performance is not affected as can be seen in the benchmark.
